sections.b: No Old Testament passage shaped the Gospel accounts of Jesus' death more than Psalm 22. Jesus cries its first line from the cross (Mark 15:34; Matthew 27:46); the passers-by shake their heads and the leaders taunt him with words close to 22:8 (Matthew 27:39–43); the soldiers divide his clothes by lot (22:18; John 19:23–24). The psalm's turn from despair to worldwide praise (22:21–31) let the first Christians read the cross and the resurrection as one story. The hard reading of 22:16, "like a lion" in the Hebrew and "they dug" in the Greek, has been argued between Jews and Christians since Justin Martyr.

common: Jesus' cry from the cross is the first line of Psalm 22.
uncommon: Some scholars hold that by quoting the first line Jesus meant the whole psalm, including its ending of victory.

sections.b: Kings of the ancient Near East called themselves shepherds of their people, and David was taken from the sheep to shepherd Israel. Psalm 23 gives the title to God and makes it personal: "The LORD is my shepherd" (23:1). The shepherd provides grass, water and rest, leads on the right tracks, and protects with club and staff in the valley of deep shadow. Psalm 28:9 asks God to shepherd and carry his people. The New Testament gives the title to Jesus, the good shepherd who lays down his life (John 10:11).

common: Psalm 23 is read at funerals in nearly every Christian and Jewish tradition.

sections.b: The title of Psalm 18 copies the narrator's line in 2 Samuel 22:1, adding "For the music director" and calling David "the LORD's servant". Psalm 22 names a tune, "The Doe of the Dawn", which the Greek read as "help at dawn" and the Talmud applied to Esther. Psalm 30 is "a song for the dedication of the house", a title that does not obviously fit its story of healing and was probably added when it was sung at the second temple or at Hanukkah. The Greek adds titles of its own: at 24:0 it has "for the first day of the week", at 27:0 "before he was anointed", and at 29:0 "at the going out of the tent". The Hebrew counts every title as verse 1.
sections.refs: Psalm 18:0; 2 Samuel 22:1; Psalm 22:0; Psalm 24:0; Psalm 27:0; Psalm 29:0; Psalm 30:0

sections.h: The king and the anointed in Psalms 18–22
sections.b: Psalms 18, 20 and 21 are royal psalms: God gives victory to "his anointed" (18:50; 20:6) and sets a gold crown on the king's head (21:3). After the kings were gone, Jewish readers heard them as promises of the coming son of David; the Targum turns "the king" of Psalm 21 into "King Messiah", and the Talmud applies 21:4 to the Messiah. Christians read them of Jesus: Paul quotes 18:49 of Christ's praise among the Gentiles (Romans 15:9). Psalm 22 is not a royal psalm in form, but the Gospels and Hebrews read it as the Messiah's suffering and vindication.
sections.refs: Psalm 18:50; Psalm 20:6; Psalm 21:1–7; Psalm 22:1–31; Romans 15:9; Hebrews 2:12

sections.h: The promise to David's line in Psalms 18 and 21
sections.b: Psalm 18 ends with the promise of 2 Samuel 7: God "shows loyal love to his anointed, to David and his line for all time" (18:50). The lamp God lights for the king (18:28) is the dynastic "lamp" promised to David's house. Psalm 21 gives the king "long days, on and on forever" (21:4), a promise later readers applied to the Messiah.

Psalms 20 and 21 are a pair: a prayer for the king before battle and thanks for his victory. They show how Israel thought about its kings: the king offers sacrifice and the people pray for him (20:3); his victory comes not from chariots and horses but from the LORD's name (20:7); his crown, long life and glory are God's gifts (21:3–5); and he stands because he trusts the Most High (21:7). The true King, the psalms say in the end, is God (20:9; 24:10).

sections.h: Psalm 22 and Psalm 28: laments that turn
sections.b: Two laments in this part change in mid-prayer from pleading to praise. Psalm 22 breaks off with "you have answered me" (22:21) and becomes a hymn for the whole world; Psalm 28 turns with "Blessed is the LORD! He has heard the sound of my pleading" (28:6). Psalm 30 tells the same story from the far side: mourning has become dancing (30:11). Scholars often explain the sudden turn by a word of assurance from a priest; readers of every age have found in it the shape of answered prayer.

sections.h: Worship at the temple in Psalms 24–29
sections.b: Psalms 24–29 are full of the temple: worshipers ask who may climb the LORD's mountain (24:3), a procession sings the King of glory through the gates (24:7–10), a worshiper washes his hands and circles the altar singing thanks (26:6–7), another longs to live in the LORD's house and look at his loveliness (27:4), another raises his hands toward the inner room (28:2), and in the temple everyone cries "Glory!" (29:9). The church took 26:6 into its Mass as the Lavabo, and the synagogue sings 24 and 29 when the Torah scroll is returned to the ark.

Psalm 19 hears the sky preaching God's glory without words; Psalm 24 says the earth is the LORD's because he founded it on the seas; Psalm 29 hears his voice in the thunder and sees him enthroned over the Flood. All three use the old picture of the world, a dome over the earth and the land set on waters, and all three deny that sun, sea or storm is a god.

Psalm 19:7–11 is the Bible's shortest hymn to the law. In six lines it names God's teaching six ways (law, decree, orders, command, fear, rulings) and says what each does: it revives, makes the simple wise, gladdens the heart, makes the eyes shine, lasts forever, and is right. It is more to be wanted than gold and sweeter than honey. Psalm 18:21–23 shows the same law kept by the king.

Psalm 18:30 calls the LORD's word "refined like metal", without impurity (quoted in Proverbs 30:5). Psalm 19 sets God's word in the law beside the wordless speech of the sky and calls it sweeter than honey.

sections.h: Sheol and the pit in Psalms 18, 28 and 30
sections.b: The king of Psalm 18 felt the ropes of Sheol and the snares of death (18:5); the speaker of Psalm 28 fears to be like those who go down to the pit (28:1); the healed man of Psalm 30 was drawn up from Sheol like water from a well (30:1–3) and argued that dust cannot praise God (30:9). Psalm 23:4's "valley of deep shadow" became, in the KJV, "the valley of the shadow of death".
sections.refs: Psalm 18:4–5; Psalm 23:4; Psalm 28:1; Psalm 30:3; Psalm 30:9; Psalm 22:15

sections.b: God answers from "his temple", his palace in heaven (18:6). On earth the temple is the place of help "from Zion" (20:2), the mountain worshipers climb (24:3), the house whose gates open to the King of glory (24:7–10), the dwelling of God's glory (26:8), the shelter where the hunted hide (27:5) and the inner room toward which hands are raised (28:2). Psalm 30's title ties it to a dedication of "the house".
sections.refs: Psalm 18:6; Psalm 20:2; Psalm 24:3–10; Psalm 26:8; Psalm 27:4–5; Psalm 28:2; Psalm 30:0

sections.h: Goodness and loyal love chase after me
sections.b: In Psalm 23 goodness and loyal love "chase after" the psalmist all his life (23:6). Psalm 25 asks God to remember his compassion and loyal love (25:6–7) and says every path of the LORD is loyal love and faithfulness (25:10). Psalm 18 ends with God's loyal love to David's line (18:50), and Psalm 21:7 says that love keeps the king from tottering.

sections.h: The LORD of Armies and the King of glory
sections.b: Psalm 24 gives the Psalter's first "LORD of Armies" (24:10), the title tied to the ark and the cherubim, and names him "the King of glory". Psalm 18:2 lists names for God from a soldier's life: cliff, fortress, rock, shield, horn, high tower. Psalm 29 calls him "the God of glory" and King over the Flood.

The speaker of Psalm 27 wants to look at how lovely the LORD is (27:4) and repeats God's own invitation, "Seek my face!" (27:8). Psalm 24 calls the worshipers those who search for God's face (24:6). In Psalm 18 God comes down in storm and darkness, hidden even as he comes (18:9–11).

Psalm 29 opens by calling the "sons of the gods" (bene 'elim) to give the LORD glory. In the Canaanite poems the sons of El are the gods; in the psalm they are God's court, bowing before him. Psalm 25:14 uses the word for God's council (sod) for his close friendship with those who fear him.

Psalm 29 describes the LORD with the images Canaanite poems used for Baal: the thunder voice, the waters, Lebanon and Sirion, the king enthroned. Since H. L. Ginsberg (1935) scholars have debated whether it adapts a hymn to Baal or answers Baal worship on purpose. Either way the psalm gives Baal's glory to the LORD.

Psalm 28:4 asks God to pay the wicked back for their deeds; Psalm 21:8–12 looks forward to the king's or God's enemies burned like a furnace and wiped out with their children. Both leave the punishment to God. Christians often pray them with Romans 12:19 in mind, as cries for justice rather than personal revenge.

Psalms 18–30 share many images with Israel's neighbors: the sun as a runner across the sky, like the Babylonian sun god Shamash (19:4–6); the storm god's voice and mountains, like Baal's at Ugarit (29); the king as shepherd, as Hammurabi called himself (23:1). In each case the psalm takes the image and denies that its subject is a god.

Psalm 18 is a warrior king's thanks to the God who trained his hands for battle (18:34). Psalm 20 says some have chariots and horses, but Israel calls on the LORD's name (20:7). Psalm 24 names the LORD "a warrior in battle" (24:8), echoing the song at the sea.

sections.h: The ark and the King of glory (Psalm 24)
sections.b: Most scholars think Psalm 24:7–10 was sung as the ark, the throne of "the LORD of Armies", was carried up to the temple. The Talmud connects it with Solomon bringing the ark into the temple, when the gates would not open until he prayed in David's name.

sections.h: The dead who bow, the man drawn up from the pit
sections.b: Psalm 22:29, as many scholars read it, has "all who sleep in the earth" bowing to God, one of the few Old Testament lines that may picture the dead worshiping. Psalm 30 thanks God for drawing a man up from Sheol, and Christians have long sung it at Easter.

Psalm 25 asks God not to remember the sins of youth but to remember the sinner in loyal love (25:7), to pardon a guilt that is huge "because of your name" (25:11), and to carry away all sins (25:18). Jews pray it in the daily supplications of the Sephardic rite and Christians in Advent and Lent.

Psalm 22:9 says God "taught me trust at my mother's breasts". The line is cited in Christian debates over whether infants can have faith and should be baptized: Lutheran teachers cite it for infant faith, while Baptists read it as God's care from birth, not saving faith.
